title: CD & Deployment Strategies
summary: Continuous delivery makes every green build releasable; continuous deployment ships it automatically. Learn the rolling, blue-green, and canary patterns that make that ship-anytime promise survivable in production.

slides.markdown:
[CI](ci-fundamentals) tells you a change is safe to merge. **Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD)** is what happens next: automating the path from a green build to production, and choosing *how* that new code meets live traffic.

That second part is the harder problem. Building and testing an artifact is deterministic; rolling it out to real users while they're actively using the system is not. A bad deploy at 2am with nobody watching can take down the service just as easily as a bad merge.

This topic covers the deployment strategies teams use to make that rollout safe: replacing instances gradually, running two environments and switching traffic, or exposing new code to a small slice of users first — each trading speed, cost, and blast radius differently.

slides.subTitle: Always releasable vs auto-released
slides.markdown:
The two terms get conflated constantly, but they mark a real decision:

- **Continuous Delivery**: every change that passes CI is automatically built, tested, and packaged into a release-ready artifact — but a human (or a scheduled process) decides when it actually goes to production. The capability to release is continuous; the act of releasing is a choice.
- **Continuous Deployment**: that last step is automated too. Every change that passes the pipeline goes to production with no human gate, often within minutes of merging.

Most teams land on delivery, not deployment, and for a defensible reason: deployment removes the last human checkpoint, which only makes sense once your automated checks (and your rollback speed) are trustworthy enough to replace a person's judgment. Continuous deployment is the more advanced practice, not the more "complete" one — it's earned, not defaulted to.

slides.subTitle: Replace instances gradually
slides.markdown:
A **rolling deployment** replaces old-version instances with new-version instances a few at a time, rather than all at once. At any moment during the rollout, both versions are serving live traffic side by side.

The mechanics: take one (or a small batch of) instance out of the load balancer, terminate or update it, bring the new version up, wait for it to pass health checks, add it back — then repeat for the next batch until every instance is on the new version.

It needs no extra infrastructure beyond what's already running, which is why it's the default in most orchestrators (Kubernetes' standard `Deployment` rollout works this way). The cost is rollback speed: undoing a bad rolling deploy means rolling the same process in reverse, batch by batch, which takes real time — and for that whole window, two versions are live, so they must be backward/forward compatible with each other.

![Rolling deployment wave moving batch by batch across six servers](assets/rolling-deploy-wave.svg)

assets.alt: Rolling deployment wave moving batch by batch across six servers

slides.subTitle: Two full environments, instant switch
slides.markdown:
**Blue-green** keeps two complete, independent production environments — call them blue (currently live) and green (idle). You deploy the new version entirely to green, test it against real infrastructure while it receives zero live traffic, then flip a router or load balancer so all traffic switches to green **instantly**.

Blue stays fully intact and idle after the switch. If something's wrong, rollback is just flipping the router back — no redeploying, no waiting for a reverse rollout. That near-instant rollback is blue-green's headline advantage over rolling.

The cost is running two full production-sized environments, at least during the switch window — roughly double the infrastructure, even if green only exists transiently. It also means no gradual exposure: every user hits the new version the moment you flip, so a bug that only shows up under real production load hits 100% of traffic at once.

![Blue-green deployment showing traffic switching from blue to green environment](assets/blue-green-switch.svg)

assets.alt: Blue-green deployment showing traffic switching from blue to green environment

slides.subTitle: Shift a small slice of traffic first
slides.markdown:
A **canary deployment** sends a small percentage of real production traffic to the new version — say 1% — while the rest continues to the old version. If the canary's metrics (error rate, latency, business KPIs) stay healthy for an observation window, the percentage steps up — 5%, 25%, 100% — until the new version fully replaces the old one.

The name comes from canaries in coal mines: a small, expendable exposure that reveals danger before it reaches everyone. The mechanism needs real traffic-splitting infrastructure (a load balancer, service mesh, or ingress that can route by percentage) and, critically, **automated metric comparison** between the canary and the baseline — without that, "canary" is just a slow rolling deployment with extra steps.

Canary catches the class of bug rolling and blue-green both miss: one that only appears under production traffic patterns, at scale, but where you'd rather 1% of users hit it than 100%.

![Canary rollout funnel widening traffic split from 1% to 100% over time](assets/canary-rollout-funnel.svg)

assets.alt: Canary rollout funnel widening traffic split from 1% to 100% over time

slides.subTitle: Risk, cost, and rollback speed
slides.markdown:
The three patterns trade the same three things in different proportions:

| Strategy | Blast radius on a bad deploy | Extra infra cost | Rollback speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rolling** | Grows with rollout progress | None — reuses existing capacity | Slow — reverse rollout, batch by batch |
| **Blue-green** | 100% instantly at the switch | ~2x during the switch window | Fastest — flip the router back |
| **Canary** | Smallest — capped at current stage % | Moderate — needs traffic-splitting + monitoring | Fast — shrink the split back to 0% |

A rough rule of thumb: reach for **rolling** when you want simplicity and can tolerate a slower rollback; **blue-green** when instant rollback matters more than infra cost (e.g. a high-traffic checkout path); **canary** when you specifically need to catch production-scale bugs before they reach everyone, and you have the monitoring maturity to detect them automatically.

They aren't mutually exclusive — a common production pattern is canary-then-rolling: validate on 1–5% with canary tooling, then roll the rest out as a standard rolling update once confidence is established.

slides.subTitle: Decoupling "code is live" from "feature is visible"
slides.markdown:
A subtlety that trips up teams new to CD: **deploying** code and **releasing** a feature are not the same event, and conflating them is what makes deployments feel scary.

Deployment means the new binary is running in production. Release means a user can actually see or use the new behavior. With a feature flag wrapping the new code path, you can deploy every day — even continuously — while the flag stays off, and release the feature separately, whenever it's actually ready, by flipping the flag rather than shipping new code.

This decoupling is why mature CD practices feel low-stakes: a deploy is "is the code running," a fully reversible, low-risk event, while "is the feature on" becomes a business or product decision made independently, often by someone who isn't even an engineer.

None of these strategies are safe without a machine watching the rollout and deciding, without waiting for a human, whether to proceed or abort. Two mechanisms do that work:

- **Health checks** (readiness/liveness probes) confirm a new instance is actually able to serve traffic before it's added to the pool — a process that started but hasn't finished loading its cache, or can't reach its database, gets held back instead of receiving live requests.
- **Automated promotion/abort** watches production signals — error rate, p99 latency, sometimes a business metric like checkout completion — during and after each rollout stage, and either advances to the next stage (5% canary -> 25%) or automatically rolls back if a threshold is breached.

The key property is that this decision doesn't wait for a human to be awake and watching a dashboard. A deploy that goes out at 2am and starts erroring should be rolled back by the pipeline itself within the observation window, not sit broken until someone notices in the morning.

slides.sectionTitle: What the numbers actually look like
slides.markdown:
A realistic canary configuration for a mid-traffic service: start at **1% for 10 minutes** (enough to catch a crash-level bug fast, on a small blast radius), then **10% for 15 minutes**, then **50% for 15 minutes**, then **100%** — roughly 40 minutes total if every stage is healthy, aborting immediately at any stage if error rate crosses a threshold like 2x the baseline or p99 latency crosses a fixed ceiling.

The stage durations aren't arbitrary — they're sized to what the metric needs to become statistically meaningful. 1% of a service doing 10,000 requests/minute is still 100 requests/minute, enough to detect a hard crash in seconds but not necessarily a subtle latency regression, which is why later stages run longer at higher percentages: the signal needs enough volume and enough elapsed time to be trusted.

For blue-green, the equivalent "stage" is the smoke-test window on green before the switch — typically minutes, running synthetic checks against real infrastructure, not real user traffic, since green isn't live yet.

The deployment strategy is only half the safety story. The other half is: **when this goes wrong, how fast can you undo it, and have you actually tested that path?**

A team that has a canary pipeline but has never once exercised the abort/rollback path in anger is often surprised to discover it doesn't work — a rollback script that references a decommissioned config, a database migration that can't run backward, or a rollback that itself takes 20 minutes because nobody optimized for that path since it "shouldn't be needed."

The practical fix is to treat rollback as a first-class, regularly-exercised capability: run it in a staging environment on a schedule, or better, occasionally trigger it for real (a deliberate rollback of a healthy deploy, just to prove the mechanism works) rather than the first real rollback being during an actual incident, under pressure, at 2am.

Every pattern above is described as if the service were stateless — swap the code, traffic follows. Real services usually own a database, and that's where the senior-level nuance lives: **the database can't be rolled out gradually the way application instances can.**

During a rolling or canary deploy, old and new application versions run concurrently against the *same* database, so any schema change must work for both versions at once — the expand/contract pattern (covered later in this group) exists specifically to make that safe. Blue-green makes this worse in one way: if blue and green point at genuinely separate databases, you've also got a data-sync problem during the switch; most real blue-green setups actually share one database and only duplicate the application tier, which reintroduces the same compatibility constraint rolling deployments have.

The interview-level takeaway: choosing a deployment strategy is really choosing how you'll manage two live app versions against one database for a window of time — the traffic-routing pattern is the visible part, the schema-compatibility discipline underneath it is what actually determines whether it's safe.
